items.abstract: <jats:p>Systems that adapt to a user's real-time state rather than treating every user identically are being built through at least three architecturally distinct strategies: distributed multi-agent reasoning, in which specialized agents divide and cross-check a task; direct physiological signal input, as in brain-computer interfaces (BCI) that adjust content delivery to a learner's measured cognitive load; and self-improving conversational agents, which adapt through accumulated interaction rather than a sensor channel. This paper compares these three strategies as they appear in a matched set of applied systems, a multi-agent tooloriented reasoning architecture, a BCI-driven language-learning platform, and an auto-improving healthcare chatbot against the broader technical literature on each approach. It finds that the three strategies differ sharply in what "adaptation" actually means and how directly it is measured: multi-agent architectures adapt reasoning structure but rarely measure user-facing outcomes directly; BCI systems measure a physiological proxy for user state with high precision but, per the strongest available controlled study, do not yet reliably translate that precision into improved learning outcomes; and conversational agents adapt through interaction history and can be evaluated against real communication-competence criteria, but adaptation quality depends heavily on design choices that are not automatic properties of the architecture. The paper argues that "adaptive AI system" is not a single design pattern but a family of approaches with different evidentiary standards, and that comparing them directly, which the literature rarely does clarifies what claim of adaptivity a given system can actually support. This paper does not present original technical benchmarks; its contribution is a comparative synthesis grounded in independently verified sources.</jats:p>
title: Architectures for Adaptive and Assistive AI Systems: Multi-Agent Reasoning, Brain-Computer Interfaces, and Conversational Agents in Education and Healthcare

items.abstract:
<jats:p>This paper presents a comprehensive survey of Quantum Multi-Agent
Reinforcement Learning (QMARL), a nascent field at the intersection of
quantum computing and multi-agent systems. The survey begins by
introducing the fundamentals of quantum computing, highlighting its
potential to revolutionize computational capabilities. We then delve
into the principles of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL),
examining how quantum computing can enhance learning efficiency and
decision-making processes in complex environments. The core of the
survey focuses on the current state of QMARL, reviewing existing
literature, methodologies, and case studies that demonstrate the
integration of quantum algorithms with MARL frameworks. The paper also
addresses the unique challenges and opportunities presented by quantum
technologies in multi-agent systems, such as quantum entanglement and
superposition, and their implications for agent coordination and
learning dynamics. Additionally, the survey explores the practical
applications of QMARL in various domains, including cybersecurity,
finance, and robotics, underscoring its transformative potential. The
paper concludes by identifying key research gaps and proposing future
directions for the development of QMARL. This includes the need for
scalable quantum algorithms, the exploration of quantum-resistant
strategies in adversarial settings, and the integration of quantum
principles in agent communication and collaboration. Overall, this
survey serves as a foundational guide for researchers and practitioners
interested in the emerging field of QMARL, offering insights into its
current achievements and future possibilities.</jats:p>
title: Quantum Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning as an Emerging AI Technology: A Survey and Future Directions

items.abstract:
<jats:p><p>The emergence of coordinated, multi-agent offensive systems in cyberspace—variously</p>
<p>manifesting as distributed reconnaissance campaigns, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery</p>
<p>pipelines, adaptive lateral movement swarms, and cross-domain settlement attacks—has</p>
<p>outpaced the formal theoretical treatment necessary for principled defence. This monograph</p>
<p>addresses that gap with five primary contributions. First, we model swarm versus counter-</p>
<p>swarm interaction as a two-player partially observable stochastic game (POSG) and derive</p>
<p>equilibrium conditions under asymmetric information. A sufficient condition is established,</p>
<p>via Fano’s inequality, under which an ambiguity-preserving offensive policy becomes dominant</p>
<p>on the induced information set; the general exact-solution problem is shown to be intractable</p>
<p>unless P = NEXP, because the POSG family strictly contains finite-horizon decentralised</p>
<p>partially observable Markov decision processes as a special case. Second, we introduce a</p>
<p>formal taxonomy of five autonomous cyber swarm attack classes—distributed reconnaissance,</p>
<p>adaptive lateral movement, threshold-splitting exfiltration, semantic service exhaustion, and</p>
<p>cross-domain settlement—each coupled to an exact detection decision problem with a worst-</p>
<p>case complexity lower bound, an information-theoretic defender error floor, and a formal</p>
<p>evasion condition. Third, we propose AEGIS-MESH (Attested Evidence-Gated Interdiction</p>
<p>System for Multi-domain Event-Synchronized HotStuff), a new counter-swarm architecture</p>
<p>specified as a process-algebraic state machine family, with Byzantine fault tolerance for</p>
<p>committees of n ≥ 3f + 1 replicas and five temporal-logic safety invariants enforcing evidence</p>
<p>gating, mandatory human approval for destructive actions, and causal auditability. Fourth,</p>
<p>we prove that the swarm attribution problem is NP-complete by reduction from Subgraph</p>
<p>Isomorphism and derive a closed-form sensor-density lower bound required to guarantee</p>
<p>attribution error at most δ. Fifth, we conduct a parametric numerical analysis of the</p>
<p>dominance condition, a systematic capability evaluation of contemporary autonomous defence</p>
<p>systems against a proposed reproducibility and external-validity framework, and a formal</p>
<p>treatment of three Web3 security problems—bridge validator-threshold compromise, blind</p>
<p>signing, and TWAP oracle manipulation—before closing with treaty-grade draft governance</p>
<p>language and an auditable definition of meaningful human control.</p></jats:p>
title: Counter-Swarm Cyber Operations: A Contemporary Analysis of Autonomous Offensive and Defensive Agent Architectures, Attack Taxonomies, and the Emerging AI Arms Race in Cyberspace

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
<jats:p>This article presents the specific case of video calling and desktop sharing (<jats:sc>vcds</jats:sc>) used in a small-scale doctoral study exploring the lesson planning processes of teachers as a result of a national curriculum change. Accessing the participants’ actions and live think-aloud exposition of their pedagogical practices also generated dialogue as new data. The study set out to explore how pedagogical content knowledge was enacted through pedagogical reasoning when participant teachers planned Computing lessons. Two central case studies captured using <jats:sc>vcds</jats:sc> are shared. One presents a dialogic research interview which developed a shared understanding of the impact of the curriculum change on one teacher’s practices. The second case study shows the potential of <jats:sc>vcds</jats:sc> to capture the verbalised thoughts and observable actions of a second teacher preparing to teach new programming skills. The video data collected provided a rich audio-visual record of the lesson planning process as it happened. This article shares the approach taken, exemplifies the data captured and reflects on <jats:sc>vcds</jats:sc> as a method for exploring teachers’ pedagogical reasoning. It concludes that, depending on the nature of the research question, <jats:sc>vcds</jats:sc> may be justified as more suitable than face-to-face, artefact-based interviews.</jats:p>
title: Internet Video Calling and Desktop Sharing (vcds) as an Emerging Research Method for Exploring Pedagogical Reasoning in Lesson Planning

items.abstract: <jats:p>This systematic review surveys advances in conversational AI from 2015 to 2025, focusing on the emergence of modular multi-agent architectures, hierarchical reinforcement learning, and self- evolving agents. A quantitative synthesis of 63 studies indicates that memory-augmented, long- horizon planners improve task success rates by approximately 30% over flat policies, while meta- learning and lifelong learning approaches halve sample complexity in data-scarce domains. Despite these gains, current systems remain brittle under distribution shifts, lack principled safety guarantees, and provide few benchmarks for diagnosing co-adaptive failure modes in mission-critical applications.</jats:p>
title: EVOLVING ARCHITECTURES AND LONG-HORIZON PLANNING IN MULTI-AGENT CONVERSATIONAL AI: A DECADE IN REVIEW

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) have become foundational to modern Artificial Intelligence (AI), enabling advanced reasoning, multimodal understanding, and scalable human-AI interaction across diverse domains. This survey provides a comprehensive review of major proprietary and open-source LLM families, including GPT, LLaMA 2, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, Falcon, and Qwen. It systematically examines architectural advancements such as transformer refinements, mixture-of-experts paradigms, attention optimization, long-context modeling, and multimodal integration. The paper further analyzes alignment and safety mechanisms, encompassing instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and constitutional frameworks, and discusses their implications for controllability, reliability, and responsible deployment. Comparative analysis of training strategies, data curation practices, efficiency optimizations, and application settings highlights key trade-offs among scalability, performance, interpretability, and ethical considerations. Beyond synthesis, the survey introduces a structured taxonomy and a feature-driven comparative study of over 50 reconstructed LLM architectures, complemented by an interactive visualization interface and an open-source implementation to support transparency and reproducibility. Finally, it outlines open challenges and future research directions related to transparency, computational cost, data governance, and societal impact, offering a unified reference for researchers and practitioners developing large-scale AI systems.</jats:p>
title: Mapping the LLM Landscape: A Cross-Family Survey of Architectures, Alignment Methods, and Benchmark Performance
